Kolky Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Kolky, Ukraine

Demolished. Jews are first recorded in Kolky from the mid-16th century, enduring hardship during the Khmelnytsky Uprising; population reached 2,537 (57.7%) by 1887, supporting four synagogues and multiple Hasidic movements (including Trisk and Stepan). A WWI fire destroyed much of the town, reducing the Jewish population to 724 (33.7%) afterward; a Tarbut Hebrew school operated until 1927, alongside four active libraries (Tarbut, Y.L. Peretz, and Bund/Poale Zion-sponsored). By late 1937, the community numbered 860. German forces arrived in July 1941, establishing a ghetto that October holding 2,500 Jews from Kolky and surrounding areas, including Polish migrants; overcrowding and unsanitary conditions bred disease before most residents were murdered in September 1942. A 1991 monument marks the mass-grave site. This cemetery, likely dating to the 16th-17th century, appears on 1880s Russian maps and was demolished during Soviet rule; per local testimony, exhumed remains were reburied in a mass grave elsewhere.
